1.text:
Why Are Inner Planets Rocky and Outer Ones Giant?

Look at the solar system and you'll spot a pattern. The four planets closest to the Sun are small and rocky. The four farthest out are huge giants. That's not an accident, and by the end of this deck you'll be able to explain why.

This is the origin story of our solar system. About 4.57 billion years ago, a cloud of gas and dust collapsed under its own gravity. It spun faster, flattened into a disk, and heated up. The Sun formed in the middle, and the planets grew in the disk around it, bit by bit.

Before we start, grab a card and take one minute: where did Earth come from? Write what you think, even if it's a guess. You'll get it back at the end to see how your idea changed.

Did you know? The ringed disk in the corner is a real young star called HL Tau, photographed in 2014. You'll see it up close near the end of this deck.

2.text:
Today I Can...

Here's the plan for this deck. Copy these into your notebook as "I can" statements so you can check yourself at the end.

I can explain how gravity turned a cloud into a hot, spinning disk and a star. I can use the frost line to explain rocky versus giant planets. I can describe accretion: dust to planetesimals to protoplanets. I can describe asteroids, comets, and the Oort Cloud as leftovers. I can explain how a giant impact made our Moon. I can explain the oddballs: Venus, Uranus, and the heavy bombardment. I can explain how meteorites give an age of 4.57 billion years. And I can use ALMA's image of HL Tau as evidence for the theory.

That's eight big ideas, each tagged with an Indiana standard or marked as enrichment. Rate yourself 1 to 3 on each now, and again at the end.

3.text:
Part 1: From Cloud to Disk

Quick challenge: name two things in the solar system that all go the same direction or lie in the same flat plane. Here's a hint. Think about how the planets travel around the Sun.

Any theory of where the solar system came from has to explain patterns like that, or it's not much of a theory. In Part 1, we'll follow the first four steps: a cold, dark cloud collapses, spins faster, flattens into a disk, and heats up. This idea goes back to Immanuel Kant in 1755 and Pierre-Simon Laplace in 1796, and modern telescopes have backed it up.

4.text:
The Solar Nebula

Space isn't totally empty. Between the stars float thin clouds of gas and dust, and our solar system started as part of one. It was cold, about 10 to 30 K, way colder than anywhere on Earth. Most of it, about 98%, was hydrogen and helium. The other 2% was heavier stuff made by earlier stars, and that small bit became the rock, metal, and ice for the planets.

When one region of the cloud got dense enough, its own gravity won out and it began to collapse inward. That collapsing piece is called the solar nebula. Look at the slide: gravity pulls everything toward the densest center.

Gravity is the engine for every step that follows. It pulls material in, and that inward fall powers the spinning, the flattening, and the heating on the next three slides.

Did you know? NASA notes that the shock wave from a nearby exploding star, a supernova, may have given our cloud the push that started the collapse.

5.text:
Spin-Up

Every real cloud has a little bit of spin. As it shrinks, that spin speeds up. Think of a figure skater: arms out, she spins slowly. Arms pulled in, she whips around fast. Nobody pushed her faster. Her spin was just packed into a smaller space.

Physicists say angular momentum stays the same. On the slide, a big, slow cloud shrinks into a small, fast one. Our solar nebula shrank from a cloud perhaps a light-year across down to a disk a few hundred AU wide, so even a lazy starting spin turned into a fast one.

That spin matters. It set the one direction that the Sun spins and that all the planets orbit.

Did you know? You can feel this yourself. Sit in a swivel chair holding heavy books out at arm's length, get a gentle spin, and pull the books in. You'll speed up!

6.text:
Flattening

Why did the cloud become a flat disk instead of staying a ball? Inside the spinning cloud, gas clumps were zooming around in all directions. Clumps moving up and down kept crashing into clumps moving the other way, and those up-and-down motions canceled out.

But the spin couldn't cancel. So the cloud squashed down into a thin, spinning disk, with a bulge in the middle where the young Sun was forming. Compare the before and after on the slide: a spinning ball becomes a flat disk where everything orbits the same way, in one plane.

That explains three patterns we see today. All the planets orbit the Sun in the same direction. Their orbits lie nearly in one flat plane. And the Sun and most planets spin in that same direction too.

Did you know? The same thing happens when a pizza maker spins a ball of dough. It spreads out into a flat disk.

7.text:
Heating

As the cloud collapsed, its gas fell inward faster and faster. All that falling gas slammed into other gas, and those collisions turned motion into heat. It's the same reason your hands get warm when you rub them together fast.

Material fell farthest and fastest near the center, so the center got hottest. That's where the protosun, the baby Sun, formed. On the slide, you can see the pattern: hottest at the protosun, warm in the middle, cold far out.

Remember that pattern. Part 2 hangs on it. The temperature at each distance decided what could freeze into solid grains there.

Did you know? The young Sun glowed long before it started fusion, just from the heat of squeezing together. And the Sun never "burns" like a fire. There's no combustion going on.

8.text:
Check for Understanding: Draw It

Time to put Part 1 together. Draw how gravity turns a cloud into a star with a disk, in 3 frames: 1) the cloud, 2) shrinking and spinning, and 3) the star with its disk.

As you draw, show gravity pulling inward, add arrows showing the spin, and label the hot center.

Keep this drawing when you're done. You'll use it again later in this deck.

9.text:
Part 2: Rock, Ice, and Gas

Here's a quick prediction. Where would you have a bigger snowball fight: in a hot classroom or a cold, snowy field? Hold on to your answer.

In Part 2, we'll see how planets grew inside the disk. The temperature pattern from Slide 7 sorted out the ingredients. Close to the Sun, only rock and metal could be solid. Farther out, past a line called the frost line, ices could freeze too. That one fact explains why rocky worlds formed inside and giants formed outside. (The picture isn't to scale!)

10.text:
The Frost Line

The frost line is the distance from the Sun beyond which ices could freeze solid. Past that point, it was colder than about 150 K, and things like water, methane, and ammonia could turn into solid ice grains. In our solar system, the frost line was between where Mars and Jupiter orbit today.

Here's why that matters. Hydrogen and helium gas, about 98% of the cloud, never froze. Ices made up about 1.4%, and rock and metal together only about 0.6%. So inside the frost line, only rock and metal could be solid. That's very little building material. Outside it, ices joined in, and there was roughly 2 to 4 times as much solid stuff to build with.

Think of a kitchen. Nothing frosts over next to the stove, but the inside of the freezer grows a coat of ice.

Did you know? In the near-vacuum of space, water vapor doesn't freeze at 0 °C like on Earth. It turns straight to ice at about 150 K, or about minus 120 °C.

11.text:
Terrestrial vs Jovian

Now we can answer the question from Slide 1. Inside the frost line, there was only a little solid material: rock and metal. So the planets there, Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars, ended up small and rocky. Their gravity was too weak to hold onto much of the hydrogen and helium gas around them.

Beyond the frost line, ices made solid material much more plentiful. Planets there built big cores of ice and rock. Once a core reached roughly 10 Earth masses, its gravity was strong enough to grab hydrogen and helium gas right out of the nebula. That's a Jovian planet: a giant whose big ice and rock core pulled in gas.

As each giant pulled in gas, the gas formed its own small, spinning disk, a mini version of the solar nebula. Moons formed in that mini disk. That's why the big moons of Jupiter and Saturn orbit the same direction their planet spins.

Did you know? Saturn is so puffed up with gas that its average density is less than water's. Earth's is about 8 times higher.

12.text:
Accretion

Accretion is how tiny grains grew into planets. Follow the stages on the slide. First, microscopic dust and ice grains bumped into each other and stuck, kind of like dust bunnies under your bed. They grew into fluffy clumps and centimeter-sized pebbles.

Pebbles stuck together into planetesimals, "small planets" about a kilometer to many kilometers across. Once bodies reached hundreds of kilometers, their gravity started pulling in neighbors. The biggest ones grew fastest. These are protoplanets, bodies on their way to becoming planets.

Finally, protoplanets crashed and merged until only a few planets were left, thousands of kilometers across. In the inner solar system, the collisions kept going until just four large bodies remained: Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars.

Did you know? For the rocky planets, this whole process took tens of millions of years.

13.text:
Sinking Iron

Big young bodies got so hot that they melted. Once they melted, heavy iron sank down to the center, and lighter rock floated up toward the top.

That's called differentiation: the body sorted itself into layers by density. Follow the three steps on the slide. It's a lot like shaking up a bottle of oil and vinegar and letting it sit. The heavy stuff settles to the bottom.

This is where an iron core comes from. Every rocky world has one.

14.text:
The Leftovers

Not every planetesimal ended up in a planet. The leftovers are still out there today: rocky asteroids and icy comets.

Asteroids are rocky leftovers from inside the frost line. Most of them orbit in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. Jupiter's strong gravity stirred things up so much there that the pieces crashed too hard to ever build a planet. Comets are icy leftovers from beyond the frost line. Icy bodies past Neptune make up the Kuiper Belt, home of Pluto.

Some icy pieces that passed close to the giant planets got flung far away in all directions. They formed the Oort Cloud, a huge, faraway shell of comets surrounding the whole solar system. (The diagram isn't to scale!)

Did you know? The asteroid belt isn't crowded like in the movies. Asteroids are typically hundreds of thousands of kilometers apart, and spacecraft fly right through.

15.text:
Check for Understanding: Jupiter vs Earth

Here's the big question from this part. Why did Jupiter grow into a giant, but Earth didn't?

Is it because A) it formed where ice was solid, so it built a big core that grabbed gas, B) it was far from the Sun's gravity, so nothing held it back, C) the Sun blew rock outward to where Jupiter was, or D) it captured gas from a passing star?

Think back to the frost line on Slide 10, pick an answer, and be ready to explain it as a chain of causes.

16.text:
Part 3: Ignition and Oddballs

A good theory explains the patterns. But what should it do about the exceptions? That's the test for Part 3.

First, we'll see how the planet-building era ended: the Sun switched on, and its powerful wind cleared out the leftover gas. Then we'll meet the rule-breakers: our unusually big Moon, Venus spinning backward, Uranus tipped on its side, and the cratered faces of the Moon and Mercury. Spoiler: rare, violent events played a big role.

17.text:
The Sun Ignites

While planets were growing in the disk, the protosun kept squeezing and heating up. When its core hit about 10 million K, something new kicked in: hydrogen fusion. Hydrogen nuclei were moving so fast they slammed together and fused into helium, releasing a huge amount of energy.

With that, our Sun was born. The Sun collected more than 99% of all the mass in the solar system. The outward push from fusion balanced gravity's inward pull, so the collapse stopped, and the Sun has been steady ever since.

To picture how hot 10 million K is: it's about 1,700 times hotter than the Sun's surface.

Did you know? If the cloud had been too small to reach 10 million K, fusion would never have started. You'd get a "failed star" called a brown dwarf instead.

18.text:
Clearing the Disk

Young Sun-like stars are rowdy. They spin fast, flare often, and blow strong winds of charged particles. Our young Sun's solar wind streamed outward and blew the leftover gas away.

Look at the slide: the gas gets pushed out, but the planets keep their solids. It's like a leaf blower on a driveway. The dust and leaves blow away, but the heavy rocks stay put. The gas was gone within a few million years.

Once the gas was gone, the giant planets couldn't grab any more, so their sizes were locked in. Jupiter and Saturn grew fast enough to capture lots of gas first. Uranus and Neptune grew more slowly and ended up with less.

Did you know? "Myr" on the slide is short for "million years."

19.text:
Where the Moon Came From

Our Moon is unusually big compared to its planet, and neither a mini disk nor a capture explains it. The leading explanation is a giant impact. About 4.5 billion years ago, near the end of planet building, a Mars-sized body named Theia struck the young, molten Earth a glancing blow.

Molten and vaporized debris flew into orbit, formed a ring around Earth, and gathered into the Moon. On the slide, the sizes are to scale, but the distances aren't.

The evidence comes from the 382 kg of Moon rocks brought back by Apollo. They show the Moon was once covered in a deep ocean of magma, and it's missing elements that boil away easily. That all fits a hot, violent birth. Moon rocks also have nearly the same chemical fingerprint as Earth rocks.

Did you know? The Moon has only a small iron core, because the debris that made it came mostly from the rocky outer layers of Earth and Theia.

20.text:
Oddball Spins

The spinning disk predicts that planets should spin the same way they orbit, with small tilts. Most do. Two don't.

Venus is tilted 177°, which means it's basically upside down, so it spins backward. It also turns at a crawl: one spin takes 243 Earth days, longer than its 225-day year. On Venus, the Sun rises in the west! Scientists aren't sure why. It could be a giant impact, slow tides from the Sun tugging on its thick atmosphere, or both.

Uranus is tilted 98°, so it rolls along its orbit on its side. It was likely knocked over by one or more giant impacts. Neither planet breaks the theory, because big collisions were common at the end of planet building.

Did you know? Venus orbits the Sun in the same direction as every other planet. Only its spin is backward.

21.text:
Heavy Bombardment

After the planets formed, plenty of leftover planetesimals were still zooming across their orbits. In the early days, impacts were far bigger and more frequent than today. Every solid world got pounded.

Earth's weather, water, and moving plates erased almost all of its early craters. But the Moon keeps the scars. Moon rocks date several giant impact basins to about 3.9 billion years ago.

Scientists still argue about whether there was a sudden spike of impacts, or whether impacts just slowly tapered off over time. Either way, the heavy bombardment was the tail end of planet building.

Did you know? Some of Earth's water may have been delivered by icy bodies that formed beyond the frost line and crashed into our planet.

22.text:
Giants on the Move

Here's an idea scientists are still testing. It's a hypothesis, not a settled fact. Young Jupiter may have moved in toward the Sun, then back out again.

Follow the three steps on the slide. Jupiter starts out past the frost line, drifts inward, then swings back out to where it is today. As it moved, its huge gravity could have thrown a lot of material out of the solar system and pulled material away from where Mars was forming.

Maybe that kept Mars small. It's a good example of an explanation built so it can be checked.

23.text:
Check for Understanding: Venus

Venus spins backward. Does that disprove the nebular theory?

Is it A) no: a rare event, like a giant impact, can change one planet, B) yes: every planet must spin exactly the same way, C) no: Venus formed around a different star, or D) yes: it proves Venus formed after the Sun died?

Choose one, and be ready to explain how a good theory handles exceptions.

24.text:
Part 4: How Do We Know?

Nobody was around 4.6 billion years ago. So how could anyone know what happened? Take a moment to brainstorm before you read on.

Scientists handle this a bit like detectives arriving long after the fact: they test their ideas against physical evidence. In Part 4, we'll look at two different kinds of clues. First, meteorites, which hold the oldest solid grains in the solar system and can be dated with radioactive clocks. Second, other young stars, where telescopes can now watch planets forming in real time.

25.text:
Radiometric Dating

Some atoms are unstable. They break down, or decay, into other atoms at a steady, known rate. That makes them good clocks. Radiometric dating reads a rock's age from how many of these radioactive atoms have decayed.

The half-life is how long it takes for half of the parent atoms to decay. Uranium-238 decays into lead-206 with a half-life of about 4.5 billion years. Follow the graph on the slide. After 1 half-life, 50% of the uranium is left. After 2, 25%. After 3, just 12.5%.

When a mineral crystal forms, it traps uranium but almost no lead. From then on, lead slowly builds up. The ratio of daughter atoms (lead) to parent atoms (uranium) is the clock. Measure it, and you know how many half-lives have passed.

Did you know? Decay rates don't change with heat or pressure. That steadiness is exactly what makes them reliable clocks.

26.text:
The Age of the Solar System

The solar system is 4.57 billion years old. That number comes from the oldest grains inside primitive meteorites called chondrites, pieces of asteroids that have barely changed since the solar nebula.

Inside those meteorites are tiny white specks called CAIs. They were the very first solids to form in the hot inner nebula. There are also chondrules, little droplets that were once melted. Dating the CAIs gives 4.57 billion years.

Earth itself is about 4.54 billion years old, a little younger, because it took tens of millions of years to finish growing. Earth's surface has melted and been recycled so much that its oldest rocks are younger still. That's why scientists turn to meteorites to find the oldest ages.

Did you know? The universe is about 13.8 billion years old, roughly three times older than our solar system.

27.text:
Watching Planets Form

If the nebular theory is right, young stars should be surrounded by flat disks of gas and dust, with planets forming inside. In 2014, a telescope array in Chile called ALMA got a sharp look at one.

The star is HL Tau, about 450 light-years away and less than about 1 million years old. Its disk is a protoplanetary disk: a disk of gas and dust around a young star, where planets form. The image shows bright rings with dark gaps between them. The leading explanation is that young planets are clearing paths through the dust as they orbit, just as the theory predicts.

ALMA sees long, millimeter-sized waves of light that pass right through the dust hiding HL Tau. The colors in the image are added by scientists, because our eyes can't see those waves.

Did you know? The planets themselves can't be seen in the image. The gaps are indirect evidence, like footprints in the snow.

28.text:
Check for Understanding: Flowchart

Time to tell the whole story yourself. Draw and caption the nebular theory in 6 boxes, following the arrows: 1) the cloud collapses, 2) a hot, spinning disk forms, 3) the frost line sorts the solids, 4) planetesimals grow into protoplanets, 5) the Sun ignites and its wind clears the gas, and 6) you get planets, moons, and small bodies.

Make sure you include the star, planetesimals, protoplanets, Jovian and terrestrial planets, moons, and small bodies. Then add 2 pieces of evidence.

Your drawing from Slide 8 already covers most of the first two boxes.

29.text:
Exit Ticket

You just built a whole solar system. Show what you've got with three quick questions.

First, why is Earth rocky but Jupiter a gas giant? Use the words frost line. Second, put these in order: protoplanet, dust grain, planet, planetesimal. Third, what do meteorites and ALMA's HL Tau image each tell us?

When you're done, look back at the card you wrote on Slide 1. How did your idea change? Then rate yourself 1 to 3 on each "I can" statement from Slide 2.

30.text:
One More Question

Here's a bonus question to stretch your thinking. Draw how a melted protoplanet ends up with an iron core.

Look back at Slide 13 if you need a hint, and label each step of your drawing.

31.text:
The Standards Behind This Lesson

This lesson follows the Indiana Earth and Space Science standards. Here's what they ask you to do, in plain words.

ES.2.1: build a flowchart with drawings that tells how the solar system formed, including the star, planetesimals, protoplanets, Jovian and terrestrial planets, moons, and small bodies. ES.2.2: describe the different kinds of objects in the solar system, know that planets have been found orbiting other stars (and even drifting with no star at all), and describe how our solar system is organized, from the rocky and giant planets to the asteroid belt and the Oort Cloud.

ES.1.3: explain how gravity pulls clouds of early elements together to form stars and galaxies. ES.5.4: tell the difference between relative and absolute ages of rocks, and between radiocarbon dating for once-living things and other radiometric dating for rocks. You'll go deeper into that one in Deck 10.
